overview: Hariphunchai was a Mon-centered kingdom around Lamphun, not the enormous country painted by this atlas. The database splits one subject into “Haripunjaya” from 1000 to 1100 and “Harapunchai” from 1200 to 1279. Their imported summaries are identical, both polygons contain Lamphun, and scholarship follows one continuing history. The later polygon even adds Chiang Saen, Kengtung, and Vientiane. They are map phases, not surveyed borders. Archaeology traces occupation from the eighth or ninth through the fourteenth century, with local development alongside Dvaravati, Pyu-Pagan, and Khmer connections. Inscriptions reveal monks, royal donors, temple workers, manuscripts, wells, pottery, spinning, and votive tablets, while ordinary voices remain scarce. The blank 1100 to 1200 interval is an editorial gap; Hariphunchai did not disappear and respawn with a spelling change. Nor did it fall in 1279 when the atlas recolored Lamphun as Sukhothai. Scholarly dates for Mangrai's takeover differ, but even the earlier 1281 date comes after that seam; the widely used date is 1292. Lan Na inherited Hariphunchai institutions and people. It was the successor kingdom, not Hariphunchai's secret earlier name.

periods.title: 750 to 850: settlement before a tidy royal story
periods.summary: Archaeology places an early Hariphunchai habitation stage in the eighth and ninth centuries, while later chronicles tell a foundation story centered on Camadevi. Material evidence confirms an emerging community and wider cultural links, but it cannot verify every person, speech, miracle, or exact year in the much later narrative.

periods.title: 850 to 950: sacred landscapes beyond Lamphun
periods.summary: Hariphunchai-style Buddhist material later appeared at San-Ku on Doi Pui, in a landscape also associated with Lawa communities. Such evidence shows religious connection across the basin without proving ethnic uniformity or political subordination. “Mon-centered” describes Lamphun's strongest written and artistic record, not every resident of the north.

periods.title: 950 to 1050: sacred images and imported connections
periods.summary: Votive imagery developed locally while drawing on artistic traditions compared with Pagan, Pala, and Gupta worlds. The atlas begins its first Haripunjaya polygon in 1000, but an object with far-reaching stylistic relatives does not establish a surveyed frontier. Lamphun's connections moved through people and ideas, not one crisp colored line.

periods.title: 1050 to 1120: inscriptions and monuments take clearer form
periods.summary: Old Mon inscriptions, votive tablets, and monuments make institutions increasingly visible around the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Royal donors, monks, artisans, sacred images, and land enter the record. The atlas removes Haripunjaya in 1100, yet the museum's inscriptional corpus crosses that software boundary without documenting a collapse.

periods.title: 1120 to 1175: the atlas gap, not a vanished kingdom
periods.summary: During the map's 1100 to 1200 gap, Lamphun's Old Mon inscriptional sequence continues across the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The museum preserves eight Old Mon records from the city. Assigning those places to a broad “Kingdom of Sukhotai” polygon does not prove conquest; the blank belongs to the map sequence.

periods.title: 1175 to 1225: votive tablets and devotional formulas
periods.summary: Small terracotta tablets from Saraphi preserve Old Mon honorifics and the names of revered monks. Repeated formulas joined writing, portable images, and merit-making in the Chiang Mai-Lamphun basin. These objects illuminate devotional practice better than population totals, household routines, or the precise reach of royal commands beyond Lamphun.

periods.title: 1225 to 1279: a late Mon kingdom before the atlas seam
periods.summary: Late Hariphunchai objects include decorated ceramics and terracotta votive tablets, while religious institutions remained active. The second atlas feature expands well beyond the evidence-supported core. Its disappearance at 1279 is especially misleading because no reviewed source records Mangrai conquering Lamphun in that year or Sukhothai instantly replacing its kingdom.

periods.title: 1279 to 1292: the color changes before the conquest
periods.summary: At 1279 the atlas assigns Lamphun to Sukhothai, yet historical chronologies place Hariphunchai's takeover later. One Smithsonian chronology gives 1281; UNESCO and recent scholarship use 1292. The disagreement deserves display, but both dates refute the map seam as a synchronized conquest or immediate Lan Na border.

periods.title: 1292 to 1350: Lan Na rule and Hariphunchai continuities
periods.summary: Mangrai's conquest brought Hariphunchai into the developing Lan Na kingdom, whose political center and composition were broader and different. Mon religious places, artisans, settlements, and inherited institutions did not evaporate. Archaeologists even trace regional ceramic production beyond the political takeover, so cultural continuity must be distinguished from sovereign continuity.

sections.title: Two atlas names, one Mon-centered history

items.text: The live index has exactly two missing records: Haripunjaya from 1000 to 1100 and Harapunchai from 1200 to 1279. Their imported summaries are byte-identical and both name Lamphun. Independent evidence supports treating the spellings as map-phase labels for one historical subject, so both ids should open this shared card.

The two polygons are not copies. The 1000 feature has fifteen ring positions and a bounding box roughly 97.58 to 102.37 east, while the 1200 feature has seventeen positions and reaches about 97.42 to 103.79 east. Shared prose is an identity decision, never a claim that these shapes are verified borders.

Both features contain fixed probes at Lamphun, Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, Wat Chamthewi, and Wiang Mano. The later polygon also adds tested Chiang Saen, Kengtung, and Vientiane. That expansion far beyond the archaeological core is why this card calls the polygons atlas envelopes instead of a growing kingdom mapped to the nearest mile.

Before 1000, the atlas assigns Lamphun to its Khmer Empire layer. At 1100, it moves Lamphun and every tested core point into a broad “Kingdom of Sukhotai” feature. At 1200, the places return under Harapunchai. No reviewed inscription or excavation identifies either software-wide transfer as a documented conquest.

All fifty tracked border snapshots were audited. Each target occurs in exactly one snapshot and one feature, with no duplicate, mixed, or out-of-lifetime target geometry. That clean database result tells us where the error lives: the records are internally consistent, but their century blocks and sweeping polygons are editorial simplifications.

sections.title: How archaeology corrects a royal legend

items.text: Later chronicles make Camadevi the invited founder of Hariphunchai, but excavated sequences must be read independently. The earliest occupation and religious material show settlement and cultural formation; they do not preserve her invitation letter, travel diary, or a founding-day ribbon. Tradition and archaeology answer different questions.

Wat Ku Kut's monuments combine Dvaravati and Lopburi-related forms with slight Pagan influence and local solutions. Art historians divide Hariphunchai production into phases rather than treating it as copied decoration. The result is a regional workshop history in which artists borrowed, adapted, and invented instead of wearing a single cultural uniform.

At San-Ku on Doi Pui, excavation found a brick vihara and stupa with eleventh to twelfth-century Hariphunchai-style votive tablets. The site lies in a landscape also associated with Lawa communities. Its objects show religious connection across the basin, but they do not turn every upland community into a Hariphunchai subject.

A Phra Perm terracotta tablet in the Hariphunchai museum is dated around the eleventh or twelfth century and shows visual relationships reaching Pagan, Pala, and Gupta traditions. Influence is evidence of connected makers and ideas, not proof that any distant court ruled Lamphun or shipped the finished tablet personally.

The Wiang Mano inscription was cut on a slate grinding stone that had already served an ordinary task. It carries Old Mon and Old Burmese writing and is dated by scholars around the eleventh or twelfth century. Reused stone links household material, religious commemoration, and regional literacy without revealing the grinder's owner.

Field archaeology places Lamphun and related settlements on the northern floodplain. Town plans could be conch-shaped or rectangular, and later phases used double earthen walls with moats. These defenses also held water, but their construction dates are not always secure enough to assign every bank and ditch to one king.

Researchers describe satellite communities such as Wiang Mano, Wiang Tha Kan, and Wiang Tho as part of an urban hierarchy linked to agricultural production and manpower. The system joined town and countryside, but surviving evidence does not calculate each village's tax, harvest, or freedom to refuse demands from Lamphun.

The Ping River shifted channels across this landscape. Geomorphology and historical texts place Hariphunchai relative to an older river course, warning us that today's map cannot simply be laid over medieval travel and farming. A river can move farther than a palace while leaving no forwarding address.

Earth walls could shelter dispersed residents during danger, according to one historical interpretation cited by the field study. That is plausible for a fortified center, yet it remains an interpretation rather than a head count from one documented siege. The card therefore distinguishes potential refuge from permanent residence inside the walls.

A Wat Saen Khao Ho inscription records a wall, Buddha images, a Bodhi tree, a coconut tree, manuscripts, and a pair of cattle. Together they show a compound tied to plants, animals, texts, and construction. They do not describe every farm or prove coconut appeared at every meal.

sections.title: Pots, thread, and useful little objects

items.text: Hariphunchai pottery changed over time: late eleventh-century jars carried radiating-star designs, early twelfth-century bodies became flatter, and thirteenth-century vessels used sloping shoulders, crosshatching, and more complex colored decoration. These sequences help date deposits while revealing makers who adjusted form and surface rather than repeating one eternal “Mon pot.”

At Wiang Mano, a slate grinding stone became the support for an Old Mon and Old Burmese inscription. Its reuse shows an ordinary tool could acquire a second, commemorative life. The object cannot tell us what was ground, who used it, or whether anyone complained about losing useful kitchen equipment.

Clay pellets may have served for hunting birds or other small animals, while little cylinders have been interpreted as protective takrut containers. Both identifications reveal possible practical and ritual uses of humble fired clay. Because function is inferred from form and comparison, the card keeps “may” firmly attached to the claim.

The late thirteenth-century Smithsonian tablet from Lamphun is terracotta, less than ten centimeters tall, and shows eighteen Buddhas. Its compact scale made a crowded sacred image portable and reproducible. Museum measurements tell us what survives; they do not name its maker, buyer, prayer, or exact place of use.

A one-line Saraphi tablet naming Bhaddiya belongs to a wider practice of impressing or inscribing sacred clay images. Terracotta could make devotion materially accessible compared with monumental stone or bronze, but the inscription does not preserve price, buyer, or distribution list. “Affordable” therefore remains a relative museum interpretation.

The Wat Don Kaew record says a king established Jetavana, provided monks' residences and scripture, and later made three stupas with two consorts, relatives, and a son. The inscription frames these acts as royal merit, yet the buildings also required unnamed planners, brickmakers, haulers, cooks, and caretakers.

The same donation assigned land and counted temple dependents, including sixteen men and twenty-two women in one group and fourteen men and thirty women serving kitchens in another. These people made institutions function, but “donated” labor signals inequality and possible unfreedom. This was not a cheerful volunteer signup sheet.

At Wat Ku Kut, an inscription connects earthquake damage with repair of Ratanacetiya. It also records land, objects, dependents, and a well built by the king's mother. A restored monument was therefore a social project involving resources and labor, not simply a tower that a ruler summoned by issuing a poetic command.

The damaged Wat Mahawan text records metal values, a named master craftsman, sacred construction, images, and temple dependents. Broken lines make some readings uncertain, so it cannot become a complete building invoice. Even fragmentary accounting is valuable because it brings skilled work and material cost beside the better-known language of royal merit.

Wat Saen Khao Ho's inscription includes a store for Tripitaka and protective paritta manuscripts alongside images, trees, a parasol, wall, and cattle. Sacred space needed storage, maintenance, animals, and landscaping as well as prayer. The record names the donor's acts more readily than the workers who watered, copied, carried, and repaired.

Written-language sample, scholarly Roman transliteration: “trala 'ey jotiyatthera.” Translation: “my Lord Jotiya Thera.” It is Old Mon incised on a terracotta votive tablet from Saraphi in the Chiang Mai-Lamphun basin, dated to the twelfth or thirteenth century. The brief label names a revered monk rather than telling a long story.

Original-script note: the period Old Mon letters survive in the published facsimile, but the reviewed editions do not supply a trustworthy machine-readable Unicode transcription of this line. Modern Mon characters would falsely replace the historical hand. This card therefore gives the secure scholarly transliteration, translation, date, place, and genre while stating the digital-script gap.

Another Saraphi tablet reads the name Pindola-Bharadvaja after the same Old Mon honorific. Several named monks on small clay objects show a shared formula and a devotional setting. They do not prove that most residents could read the labels or that every monastery taught the same curriculum.

Wat Saen Khao Ho records stores for Tripitaka and paritta manuscripts beside religious images and a compound wall. These details establish texts and specialist learning, while no reviewed source supplies a school timetable, classroom plan, examination, or enrollment list for ordinary girls and boys.

The Hariphunchai National Museum reports twenty-six inscriptions in its collection, eight in Old Mon and all of those from Lamphun. That corpus anchors Mon literacy locally, but museum survival is selective. Stone and fired clay endure better than palm leaf, conversation, memory, or a child's practice marks in dust.

sections.title: Families, status, and children's missing voices

items.text: The Wat Don Kaew donor names two consorts, other relatives, and a son in making stupas. The king's mother appears separately at Wat Ku Kut as builder of a monastery well. These records reveal elite kin acting through religious gifts, but they cannot stand in for ordinary marriage, inheritance, affection, conflict, or caregiving.

Men and women both appear among assigned temple dependents and kitchen workers. The lists prove gendered people performed institutional labor; they do not reveal consent, family grouping, pay, age, living conditions, or whether children accompanied adults. Counting workers is not the same as hearing their lives, and the distinction matters.

A donated pair of cattle at Wat Saen Khao Ho linked sacred merit with everyday animal care. Someone still had to feed, water, shelter, and manage the animals after the formal gift. The inscription records the donation, not the herder's name, workload, ownership rights, or whether milk entered local diets.

Children are almost absent from the reviewed Hariphunchai sources. A royal son appears as a donor, but no secure text describes childbirth, toys, games, discipline, apprenticeships, age grades, or daily lessons. Skills clearly passed between generations; the record does not tell us whether that happened at hearth, workshop, field, or monastery.

Religious donors, rulers, monks, master artisans, and dependent workers appear because institutions recorded them unevenly. Farmers, potters, carriers, caregivers, and builders are often inferred from products and projects rather than named. Hariphunchai society was not only a royal family portrait; the surviving frame simply favors people near monuments and gifts.

A king's mother built a well inside a monastery, giving the clearest secure glimpse of managed water in the reviewed inscriptions. The well served an institution, but its record does not explain lifting devices, water quality, access rules, household supply, or dry-season shortages. One well cannot become a citywide plumbing diagram.

Moats around northern settlements could also function as reservoirs. That combination joined defense and water storage, while changing river channels and floodplain conditions shaped local risk. Neither feature proves that water was safe to drink, continuously available, or distributed equally among residents inside and outside the walls.

No reviewed Hariphunchai source securely identifies a physician, pharmacy, hospital, diagnostic manual, surgical instrument, childbirth treatment, or medicine recipe between 750 and 1350. People certainly cared for illness and injury, but later Lan Na medical manuscripts cannot be quietly moved backward and relabeled as Mon kingdom practice.

No securely dated toilet, latrine, sewer, cesspit, or written waste rule appears in the surveyed Hariphunchai evidence. Wells, moats, pots, and walls are not automatic sanitation systems. Archaeology has not issued this kingdom a plumbing certificate, which says more about preservation and research than about whether people valued cleanliness.

Food remains frustratingly indirect. The donation records count kitchen workers and land without preserving recipes or a universal menu. Pots survive better than lunch. The sources do not securely tell us ordinary meal frequency, child feeding, alcohol use, famine foods, preferred flavors, or who ate first.

A Phra Perm tablet belongs to a connected Buddhist visual world, with features compared to Pagan, Pala, and Gupta traditions. Similarity can follow artisans, models, pilgrims, gifts, or shared beliefs. It should not be flattened into an arrow saying one distant kingdom politically owned Lamphun.

A Wiang Takan plaque depicts the Buddha's birth with features comparable to Pagan art while retaining a locally distinctive water-pot detail. That combination is an achievement in adaptation: makers could speak a shared religious visual language and still choose local forms. Connected art was creative work, not photocopying before photocopiers.

The atlas gives Haripunjaya direct shared arcs with Khmer Empire, Dvaravati, and Pagan features in 1000. In 1200, Harapunchai touches Nan Chao, Ai Viet, a Mon State feature, Khmer Empire, and Bagan. These are tiling relationships in imported geometry, not proof of alliances, wars, tribute, or direct diplomacy.

Old Burmese beside Old Mon at Wiang Mano and Pagan-related imagery elsewhere show meaningful east-west connections. They do not erase local Mon evidence or make Hariphunchai a province of Pagan. Multilingual and stylistically connected objects are strongest when read as movement of people and ideas, with the exact route left open.

Hariphunchai's achievement was more than royal survival. The damaged Wat Mahawan record preserves metal values, a master craftsman, sacred construction, images, and dependent labor. It reveals institutions that mobilized skill and resources while resting on hierarchy. Accomplishment and inequality belong in the same account, not separate display cases.

At the 1279 snapshot, Lamphun, Chiang Mai, Lampang, Sukhothai, Phayao, Chiang Rai, Chiang Saen, and Vientiane switch from Harapunchai to the atlas's Sukhothai feature. Kengtung, Mae Hong Son, and Doi Inthanon switch to Pagan. This sweeping repaint is internally exact and historically unsynchronized.

The 1300 snapshot repeats those assignments, even though scholarship places Mangrai's takeover of Hariphunchai in the intervening years. The atlas therefore fails twice: it makes Sukhothai the immediate owner in 1279 and then leaves the Lamphun core there after the better-attested Lan Na conquest.

Sources disagree on the takeover year. The Smithsonian chronology gives 1281, while recent historical scholarship uses 1292. Neither supports a fall in 1279. This card presents the disagreement instead of averaging it into 1286.5, a date impressively precise and historically rather silly.

After annexation in 1292, Mangrai's dynasty developed a broader Lan Na kingdom and founded Chiang Mai in 1296. Mon Hariphunchai institutions and people formed one inheritance within that new political order. Calling earlier Hariphunchai “Lan Na” would reverse the sequence and hide what the conquering kingdom absorbed.

Ceramic production and sacred activity continued after political takeover. That continuity does not mean sovereignty never changed; it means potters, monks, workers, families, and places outlasted a royal transfer. The card ends with continuity, leaves the 1279 fall field null, and names no synchronized Sukhothai successor at the map seam.

ending.text: The atlas removes “Harapunchai” in 1279 and recolors Lamphun as Sukhothai, with several western upland points assigned to Pagan. No reviewed history describes that synchronized transfer. Independent chronologies place Mangrai's conquest later, in 1281 or 1292. Both dates show that 1279 is an editorial seam, not the kingdom's documented fall. Mangrai's conquest ended Hariphunchai's independent Mon monarchy and folded its core into the emerging Lan Na kingdom, while people, monasteries, artisans, texts, settlements, and ceramic traditions continued. Lan Na was a new composite polity that inherited Hariphunchai institutions; it was not the earlier kingdom under another spelling. The 1100 to 1200 blank is likewise a map gap, not extinction and rebirth. Because the target records end before the disputed takeover, both overrides leave fell null and name no successor at 1279. The card preserves the later conquest without letting the software conquer anyone early.
